slides.title: Exponent Laws with Variable Bases
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the bridge: y · y · y · y · y is y⁵ for exactly the reason 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 is 2⁵. A student who can write that can do every law in this lesson by expanding. Q1 is yesterday's skill and the same skill as today's with the letters swapped in.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Expand once, from the front: x² is x · x, x³ is x · x · x, so the product is five x's. The law is the one they know; the only change is that nothing gets 'evaluated' at the end — x⁵ is the answer. Then the coefficients: 3x² · 5x⁴ is 3 · 5 · x² · x⁴. Coefficients multiply; exponents add. Say the two wrong boards out loud before they appear: 15x⁸ (multiplied the exponents) and 8x⁶ (added the coefficients).
OFF: 'Coefficients multiply. Exponents add. Two different operations in the same problem.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
(x³)⁴ is four copies of x³, twelve x's: multiply. Then the power of a product, where the coefficient is the thing students forget to raise: (2y²)³ is 2y² · 2y² · 2y², so the 2 is cubed too. The state guide's task is the pair Rachel/Justina: (15xy²)³ expanded as 15·15·15·x·x·x·y·y·y·y·y·y and written as 3,375x³y⁶ are the same expression. Both are correct; one is finished.
OFF: 'Everything inside the parentheses gets the exponent — the number included.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: x⁷ over x² cancels two x's and leaves five: subtract. Coefficients divide as numbers; each variable is handled on its own. Today every quotient comes out with positive exponents (or a zero exponent, which is 1) — tomorrow the subtraction is allowed to go below zero. Note the last line: n⁴/n⁴ is n⁰ = 1, not 0 and not n.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Three kinds of factor in each monomial: a coefficient, x's and y's. Ask what happens to each kind before anyone writes.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Regroup by kind, then apply the product law twice. The y in the first factor has exponent 1 — a board with y⁵ forgot it. A board with −8x⁶y⁵ multiplied the exponents; a board with 2x⁵y⁶ added the coefficients.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the missing exponent 1 on a and the exponent-multiplier (15a²b⁸). 15a³b⁶ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A power of a product, then a quotient.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Two laws in order: the numerator is a power of a product, then divide. Ask which law comes first and why (the exponent outside the parentheses has to be dealt with before anything can be divided).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Raise every factor in the numerator: 3³ = 27, (m²)³ = m⁶, n³. Then divide the coefficients and subtract each variable's exponents. A board with 3m⁶n³ on top never cubed the 3; a board with 3m²n³ forgot the n in the denominator.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the un-raised coefficient (2p¹²/8p⁵ = p⁷/4) and the exponent-adder (2p⁹). 2p⁷ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

A student who picks Justina alone has not seen that the two are the same expression; one who picks Rachel alone thinks the 15 should not be cubed.
